title: Bacteria
summary: Bacteria are tiny single-celled living things that are everywhere - in soil, water, on our skin, and in our guts. Explore their simple cell structure, how they divide, and how some help us while a few can make us sick.

compareCandidate.label: Bacteria vs. virus
compareCandidate.description: Bacteria are tiny single-celled living things that can grow and divide on their own. Viruses are much simpler and are not cells; they must commandeer a living cell to reproduce.

plainLanguageExplanation: Bacteria are tiny organisms made of just one cell - some so small that thousands could rest on a pencil point's tip. A bacterial cell is simple and has no nucleus; its DNA floats freely. It reproduces by splitting in two (binary fission), and can divide very quickly. Bacteria live every kind of place on earth - soil, water, and even in our bodies. Most are harmless, many are helpful (they help digest food, make yogurt and soil fertile), and only a small fraction can make us sick, but those we treat with antibiotics.

whyItMatters: Bacteria are the most common life forms on Earth and shape our health and the planet. They help digest food, make nutrients in soil, and make food like yogurt - and understanding them explains infection, antibiotics, and why washing your hands matters.
tagline: The tiniest, most common living cells
didYouKnow: There may be billions of individual bacteria in a single gram of soil, each one a separate living cell.
